answer.label: Not Einstein — popularized by
answer.sourceLine: One of the most-shared “Einstein” quotes — but he died in 1955, decades before it appeared. It arose anonymously in 12-step recovery culture around 1981; novelist Rita Mae Brown put a near-identical line in print in 1983.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: Oct 11, 1981 — an Al-Anon meeting report in the Knoxville News-Sentinel
Rita Mae Brown, Sudden Death (1983), p. 68 — not credited to Einstein

source.excerpt: Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.
source.cutTag: ↑ the “Einstein said…” framing was grafted on later
source.excerptNote: Einstein died in 1955 — about 26 years before this saying is first documented. It appears nowhere in his writings, and Alice Calaprice's authoritative The Ultimate Quotable Einstein lists it under “Misattributed to Einstein.”

sourceLink.text: Read the full chronology at Quote Investigator

trail: Earliest strong match: an unnamed Al-Anon attendee quoted in the Knoxville News-Sentinel, Oct 11, 1981 — documented and dated by Quote Investigator.
A near-simultaneous variant appears in the Narcotics Anonymous “Basic Text” (Nov 1981): “Insanity is repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results.”
Popularized in print by Rita Mae Brown in Sudden Death (1983, p. 68) — sourced on Wikiquote; she did not credit Einstein.
Listed as misattributed in Calaprice's Ultimate Quotable Einstein, and rated false by Snopes; even the verified Einstein Facebook page disavowed it in 2014.
source.rightsNote: Usage & rights: This is anonymous folk wisdom from recovery culture — there's no author to credit, and no basis for the Einstein attribution. If you must attribute it, “origin unknown; popularized by Rita Mae Brown (1983)” is the honest form.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says Einstein
misattribution.intro: It's one of the most-shared fake Einstein quotes on the internet. Here's why it isn't his:

items.why: He died in 1955 — about 26 years before the saying is first documented (1981). It's absent from his writings and is listed under “Misattributed” in the authoritative The Ultimate Quotable Einstein. Debunked by Snopes ↗
Sometimes guessed in attribution debates, but no researcher finds any Franklin connection. History.com ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The real chain: anonymous 12-step recovery culture (Al-Anon / NA), 1981 → into print via Rita Mae Brown, 1983 → grafted onto Einstein's name by about 1990. The full chronology ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line became a cornerstone slogan of American recovery culture — a compact way for Al-Anon, AA, and Narcotics Anonymous members to name the self-defeating loop of addiction and to motivate change. That therapeutic punch is exactly why it traveled so far beyond recovery rooms into management, politics, and self-help.
context.pull: Attaching an anonymous truism to a genius launders it into settled wisdom.
detailsBody: Its migration onto Einstein's name is a textbook case of how misquotation works: a prestige name makes an aphorism feel authoritative, and the misattribution then becomes near-impossible to dislodge. Einstein is a magnet for any pithy line about thinking or rationality.
It's a standard exhibit in fact-checking literature — Snopes, History.com's “6 Things Einstein Never Said,” and the MLA Style Center all use it to explain the mechanics of viral misquotes.

author.name: Rita Mae Brown
author.heading: About Rita Mae Brown
author.metaLine: American novelist · b. 1944 · put the line in print in 1983
author.bio: Rita Mae Brown (b. 1944) is an American novelist and memoirist, best known for Rubyfruit Jungle (1973). Her 1983 tennis-world mystery Sudden Death contains the earliest widely-read print version of the “insanity” line — voiced by a character, and pointedly not credited to Einstein. The saying itself arose anonymously in 12-step recovery communities around 1981.
